before: **2. Weekly stayer (Wochenaufenthalter) and others who lose commuter status.** A German resident with a weekday room in Switzerland who stays there on more than 60 working days is not a commuter. Art. 15 applies instead: Switzerland may tax pay for work done in Switzerland. Germany exempts that pay but uses it to set the rate on other income (art. 24(1) no. 1(c) and no. 2; § 32b(1) no. 3 EStG). Germany grants the exemption only if the person proves that Switzerland taxed the pay and the tax was paid, or that Switzerland waived its right (§ 50d(8) EStG). Pay for workdays spent outside Switzerland stays taxable in Germany.
after: **2. Weekly stayer (Wochenaufenthalter) and others who lose commuter status.** After actual commuter status fails, test art. 15(2) before allocating Swiss work pay under art. 15(1): pay remains taxable only in the residence state if presence in the other state is not more than 183 days in the relevant calendar year, the actual treaty employer is not resident there, and its permanent establishment there does not bear the remuneration. Count presence days, not just working days; establish employer and any economic-employer issue from the actual facts. An ordinary German-resident non-commuter present for 80 days in Switzerland for an actual German treaty employer, with no Swiss permanent establishment bearing the pay and all other stated gates met, stays exclusively German-taxable on that pay. At 184 days or with a Swiss-resident employer, that exception fails; then art. 15(1), subject to the other actual special rules, allows Swiss taxation of pay for work there. Germany exempts qualifying pay with progression (art. 24(1) no. 1(c), no. 2; § 32b(1) no. 3 EStG), only on proof either that Switzerland waived its taxing right or that Swiss tax assessed on the pay was paid (§ 50d(8)); a bare zero-withholding certificate does not itself establish a waiver. Under that ordinary art. 15(1) workday route, pay for days outside Switzerland stays German-taxable. Existing examples with a Swiss employer do not meet art. 15(2)(b).

after: **4. Germans who move to Switzerland.** Moving alone does not end German domestic unlimited liability: test any retained German home or habitual abode under § 1(1) EStG separately from treaty residence. If that domestic liability actually ends, four German departure rules can follow:

before: - **Treaty tail, art. 4(4).** A Swiss resident without Swiss nationality who was fully taxable in Germany for at least five years in total remains taxable in Germany on German-source income in the year their German liability ended and the five following years. Germany credits the Swiss tax on that income. This does not apply to someone who moved to take up genuine employment with an employer in which they have no substantial interest. A German employer may not apply the 4.5% cap to such a person while art. 4(4) applies (Gre-1 note 3).
after: - **Treaty tail, art. 4(4).** A Swiss resident without Swiss nationality who was fully taxable in Germany for at least five years in total remains taxable in Germany on German-source income in the year their German liability ended and the five following years. The separate art. 4(4) credit, under the actual German foreign-tax-credit rules and excluding trade tax, covers treaty-permitted Swiss tax only against the additional German tax imposed by this tail beyond what arts. 6–22 otherwise permit. Stipulated German tail tax EUR 300, otherwise treaty-permitted German tax EUR 100 and otherwise eligible Swiss tax EUR 250 give an additional-tax cap of EUR 200, credit EUR 200 and German remainder EUR 100. These are independently established inputs, not an official example or the full commuter § 36 settlement credit. This does not apply to someone who moved to take up genuine employment with an employer in which they have no substantial interest. A German employer may not apply the 4.5% cap to such a person while art. 4(4) applies (Gre-1 note 3).

before: - The 2026 tariff applies to taxable income, with the solidarity surcharge at 5.5% above the EUR 20,350 threshold of income tax (see de-employee-income-tax).
after: - The 2026 tariff applies to taxable income. For ordinary assessment without a separate § 32d(3)/(4) component, establish the actual Soli base and threshold: EUR 20,350 for a single assessment, EUR 40,700 for the statutory joint cases. Up to that threshold the ordinary surcharge is zero; above it take the smaller of 5.5% of the base and 11.9% of its excess over that threshold, dropping fractions of a cent. A stipulated ordinary single base of EUR 20,400 gives min(EUR 1,122, EUR 5.95) = EUR 5.95. Use the employee companion for child-related base and special § 32d selectors; Swiss § 36 withholding credit is a settlement credit, not a reduction of this Soli assessment base.

before: - Pay for work days in Switzerland: Swiss tax under art. 15; exempt in Germany with progression (art. 24(1) no. 1(c), no. 2; § 32b EStG), only with proof of Swiss tax paid (§ 50d(8)).
after: - After testing art. 15(2) and other actual special rules above, qualifying Swiss workday pay under art. 15(1) is exempt in Germany with progression (art. 24(1) no. 1(c), no. 2; § 32b), on proof of Swiss waiver or payment of assessed Swiss tax (§ 50d(8)). If the three art. 15(2) gates instead hold, do not exempt that pay merely because work occurred in Switzerland.

after: Protocol no. 9 covers Swiss second-pillar insurance payments where the last or current employment relevant to that insurance relationship before payment/start was in Swiss public service, including the specified vested-benefit accounts/policies. after: - **Late filing surcharge (§ 152 AO).** 0.25% per started month of the assessed tax less prepayments and credited withholding, at least EUR 25 per month, at most EUR 25,000. The § 152(2) compulsory route after 29 February 2028 is subject to § 152(3): it does not apply where the office extends the deadline under § 109, including retroactively, where assessed tax is zero or negative, or where assessed tax does not exceed assessed prepayments plus creditable withholding. These exceptions limit paragraph 2 compulsion; apply paragraph 1's separate discretionary conditions, not an automatic waiver of every surcharge.

before: - **Lost commuter status found late.** The employer must collect the Swiss tax not withheld (Gre-1 note 4). In Germany the exemption under art. 24 is refused until the Swiss tax is shown paid (§ 50d(8) EStG), so the return is assessed with the pay taxed and changed later.
after: - **Lost commuter status found late.** The employer must collect the Swiss tax not withheld (Gre-1 note 4). In Germany where art. 24 exemption actually applies after the other treaty tests, § 50d(8) requires proof either of Swiss waiver or that Swiss assessed tax was paid. If the required proof is first supplied after the German assessment included the pay, amend that assessment to the corresponding extent; do not demand payment of tax where a valid waiver is proved.

before: - **Swiss withholding for German residents, dividends, interest.** Switzerland withholds 35% Verrechnungssteuer; under art. 10 a German resident can recover down to 15% (0% for a German company holding at least 10% for 365 days); interest is taxable only in Germany (art. 11). after: - **Swiss withholding for German residents, dividends, interest.** Switzerland withholds 35% Verrechnungssteuer. For the treaty-resident beneficial owner, the ordinary residual dividend ceiling is 15% under art. 10(2)(c); separately classify the Rhine border-power-company 5% population and the specified deductible silent-participation/profit-sharing instruments under the 30% branch in (a)/(b). Art. 10(3) gives source-state exemption only to a beneficially entitled treaty-resident company other than a partnership, directly holding at least 10% for a 365-day period including the dividend payment day; the stated merger/division/conversion changes are disregarded for that period. Indirect 10%, partnership ownership or an unproved payment-inclusive period does not establish zero. Its German REIT/fund exclusion concerns German payers; do not extend it to Swiss payers. Actual entitlement and evidence precede any Swiss refund, whose route is in ch-cross-border; German outbound cases use the treaty-withholding companion. Interest follows art. 11's separate Germany-only route.
